name: Quit smoking for teeth

lead: Smoking leaves tar stains on the tooth surface, usually yellow to brown near the gumline. Stopping removes the source of new staining and is linked to better gum health.
Communities treat it as a free baseline step before whitening or veneers.

paras: Tobacco tar deposits on enamel as extrinsic stain. Without ongoing exposure, no new deposits form; existing stain is typically removed by scaling and polishing or abrasive toothpaste.
No risks from quitting itself are described in the sources. No trial has measured tooth colour change after cessation. Smoking is associated with periodontitis, tooth loss and leukoplakia.

lead: Quitting smoking for teeth refers to stopping tobacco use as a way of preventing or reducing the yellow-brown-black staining and other oral changes associated with smoking. Tar from smoke and smokeless tobacco forms a stain on the tooth surface, typically near the gumline, which dental references classify as extrinsic (surface) discolouration.[1]

Existing extrinsic stains are generally removed by cleaning, either with abrasive toothpaste at home or by professional scaling and polishing, while identifying and removing the cause, such as smoking, is described as necessary to prevent the stain returning.[1] A dental survey study has also noted that smoking affects oral health in several ways, including periodontitis, tooth discolouration and oral cancer, and proposed that oral health complaints can be an opening for cessation counselling.[2]
In looksmaxxing terms the practice is a low-cost lifestyle measure rather than a procedure. No published trial has specifically measured how much tooth colour changes after quitting.
infobox: Professional scaling and polishing, tooth whitening

paras: Tobacco staining sits on the outside of the enamel and is distinct from intrinsic discolouration, which arises within the tooth from causes such as tetracycline exposure or fluorosis.[1] Quitting removes the ongoing source of new tar deposits, but removal of established stain is typically done by cleaning rather than by cessation alone.[1]

Smoking is described as an important factor in teeth staining, and smokers are two to three times more likely to lose teeth. About half of periodontitis cases are linked to current or past smoking, and smokers show greater bone height loss than non-smokers.[3] Smoking can also cause white patches called leukoplakia, and smokeless tobacco is associated with gum recession.[3]
The general encyclopedia article on tobacco's health effects does not state to what degree quitting reverses staining, gum damage or bone loss.[3]

No studies found that measure tooth-shade change after smoking cessation as an outcome. A 2010 questionnaire study in a dental setting examined whether oral health complaints could be used as a prompt to start smoking cessation counselling.[2]
